title: Exams stay AI-free, even where homework is open
body: The most uniform rule in the corpus. Courses that welcome AI on projects still close it off on exams, quizzes, and in-class work. Many are moving more of the grade onto those unassisted settings.

title: Students own what they submit and must be able to explain it
body: Whatever the default stance, policies converge on accountability. The student is responsible for correctness and must be able to explain or defend every line, sometimes in a live interview.

title: Learning, not productivity, is the stated reason for limits
body: Restrictions are justified almost entirely in terms of skill-building. AI is described as skipping the practice that produces learning, as especially harmful to novices, and as hiding gaps that show up later on exams.

title: Misuse is handled through existing academic-integrity processes
body: Few policies invent new enforcement. Unauthorized AI use is treated as plagiarism or unauthorized collaboration, reported through the usual channels, and penalized with familiar sanctions.

title: Where AI is allowed, disclosure is the price of use
body: Permissive policies almost always attach a disclosure duty. Its form varies: a statement, a citation with the prompt, the full transcript, or a comment at the exact lines.

title: AI as a tutor is the most widely permitted use
body: Even restrictive courses typically allow AI for explaining concepts, error messages, and course material. The usual line falls between asking questions and getting answers.

title: Universities delegate; computing units decide
body: University-wide policies mostly hand the decision to instructors: about half defer explicitly to the instructor and about a quarter offer a menu of use levels. Their concrete rules concern syllabus statements, data privacy, and doubts about detectors. Computing departments and courses make the substantive calls themselves: whether code may be generated, whether AI is allowed on exams, and whether students must explain every line. A university policy alone rarely tells a computing student what is allowed.

title: Default stance: prohibit or embrace?
body: Courses at the same level, sometimes in the same department, take opposite defaults. Some rule AI out entirely for graded work; others build the course around AI coding agents.

title: Does disclosure make use acceptable?
body: Some policies promise that honest disclosure carries no penalty, so nondisclosure becomes the offense. Others hold that disclosed use is still a violation or still earns no credit.

sides.label: Disclosed use can still be penalized

title: Detecting AI: disavow detectors or deploy them?
body: Some institutions state that AI detectors are unreliable and promise not to use them. Others say they run tools that look specifically for AI-generated code or text.

title: Career readiness versus foundational skill
body: The same appeal to future employment is used on both sides. Some argue graduates must be fluent with AI; others argue employers will keep testing unassisted ability, so the fundamentals must come first.

title: Treat AI like a person, or write AI-specific rules?
body: One family of policies maps AI onto existing collaboration rules: if you couldn't ask a friend, don't ask the model. Another writes rules only AI needs, such as word caps on prompts, line limits, percentage caps, and bans on tools reading the codebase.

title: Monitoring the process versus protecting student data
body: To verify authorship, some courses log prompts, sessions, or commit histories. Others warn students that AI services store and profile what they are given. Process evidence and privacy pull in opposite directions.

title: Should instructors grade with AI?
body: Policies that address faculty use disagree. Some commit that AI will never grade; one discloses AI-assisted grading and offers an opt-out.

title: Who sets the rule: the instructor or the department?
body: Many units defer entirely to each instructor. A few impose a shared tier system or department-wide rule, trading local flexibility for consistency students can rely on.

title: AI for prose: never, or freely?
body: Writing gets its own rules, but in opposite directions. Some computing courses allow only spelling and grammar checkers; some information-school courses let students generate or rephrase text.

title: Faculty and TA use of AI is rarely addressed
body: Nearly every document regulates students. Only a handful say anything about how instructors may use AI for grading, feedback, or course materials, or commit to disclosing it.

title: Equity, cost, and accessibility are seldom mentioned
body: Few policies consider students who cannot pay for premium tools, who prefer a human, or who rely on assistive technology with built-in AI.

title: Amnesty and self-reporting are rare
body: Almost all enforcement language is punitive. Only a few courses offer a window to come forward or withdraw a submission.

title: Agentic tools are only starting to appear
body: Most policies still picture a chatbot. A few address IDE-embedded assistants and autonomous agents that read and edit a whole codebase, a fast-moving area where most policies are silent.

title: Little evidence, little revision
body: Policies make strong claims about learning, but few cite their own course data or commit to reviewing the policy on a schedule.

title: Ethical, environmental, and IP concerns are peripheral
body: Bias, labor, energy use, and licensing appear in only a few documents, and rarely as rules.
